title: Lancaster Street West towers approved despite opposition
subtitle: Also: Weber and King Street mixed-use projects, Compass Kitchener report card, Roos Island encampment delegations, park land swap.
overview: Council approved the Official Plan and zoning changes for a large rental development at 528-550 Lancaster Street West and 26 Bridge Street West {{vote:m1}}. Amendments replaced the relocation of two older homes with commemoration and community benefits the developer offered: a park contribution, a donation to the Working Centre, housing options for current tenants, and affordable units. A holding provision keeps development on hold until the Region reviews traffic, and an alternate access toward Riverbend Drive is to be explored.

Council also approved mixed-use projects at 1157 and 1175 Weber Street East and at 1770 King Street East, the latter requiring ground-floor commercial space. Other approvals covered 67 and 71 Nelson Avenue, a noise exemption for downtown special events, a self-employment program agreement with the Region, and the Kitchener Utilities clean energy transition approach.

After a closed session, council passed a resolution on a land swap with the Grand River Conservation Authority: surplus road allowance parcels at Chicopee are to be sold and Walter Bean Trail parcels at Deer Ridge acquired. Council also heard delegations on the Roos Island encampment and received the Compass Kitchener report card on the 2019-2022 strategic plan.

decisions.item: 528-550 Lancaster St W and 26 Bridge St W
decisions.detail: Council adopted the Official Plan amendment and approved the zoning changes with amendments accepting commemoration and community benefits instead of moving two homes, a traffic-related holding provision and a study of an alternate Riverbend Drive access {{vote:m1}}.
Council changed the land use from Commercial to Mixed Use, approved the zoning and endorsed the urban design brief for a mixed-use development.

decisions.item: 1770 King St E and 815/825 Weber St E
decisions.detail: Council approved a 27-storey residential development with required ground-floor commercial space of at least 650 square metres and higher ground-floor ceilings.
Council approved an amended zoning change and granted draft condominium approval, subject to conditions.

decisions.item: Chicopee and Walter Bean Trail land swap
decisions.detail: Council declared the Chicopee road allowance parcels surplus and authorized sale to the GRCA and purchase of the Walter Bean Trail at Deer Ridge parcels.
Council endorsed the project phases and approach for the transition outlined in the staff report.
Council authorized staff to sign funding and participant agreements with the Region for the Self Employment Ontario Works program.
Council granted an exemption from the noise bylaw for downtown special events listed in the staff report.

debate: Delegates opposed to the Lancaster development raised environmental concerns about the Grand River corridor, tree loss and a narrowly scoped environmental study, and said Six Nations had not been consulted on land within the Haldimand Tract.

Nearby residents said traffic on Lancaster Street is already hard to enter and exit, questioned the traffic studies, and asked for more parking, a smaller project and an alternate entrance. Staff said the holding provision requires the Region to review a left-turn lane and the transportation study before development proceeds.

Tenants said the replacement units offered were smaller and unsuitable, including for a home studio, and that five years at current rent does not solve displacement. The developer said it offered comparable units and affordable units and would keep working with each tenant.

Several councillors said they disliked the project or its location but supported it because a refusal could be appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal, risking the offered benefits and adding costs. One councillor voted against, arguing council should not fear the tribunal and that traffic and environmental issues were unresolved.
Staff said deferral would count as a non-decision that could be appealed, and that the holding provision was the only tool to require further study.
